question: A 10-year-old boy presents with a swollen, red right eyelid for 2 days following an upper respiratory tract infection. On examination, he has lid oedema and erythema but moves his eye freely in all directions with no pain on movement, no proptosis, and normal visual acuity. Which of the following features would MOST reliably indicate orbital rather than preseptal cellulitis?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Bilateral involvement is more characteristic of cavernous sinus thrombosis (CST) — a feared complication of orbital cellulitis — not of orbital cellulitis itself, which is typically unilateral.

answers.text: Restricted and painful extraocular movements with proptosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Restricted, painful extraocular movements with proptosis indicate involvement of post-septal (orbital) soft tissues — i.e. orbital cellulitis (Chandler class II+). The orbital septum is the critical anatomical barrier; once infection crosses it, the extraconal and intraconal spaces are involved, restricting ocular motility and displacing the globe anteriorly.

Pyrexia can accompany both preseptal and orbital cellulitis; it is not the distinguishing feature between the two. Higher fever may suggest a more severe infection but alone does not localise it as post-septal.

Lacrimal sac tenderness is a feature of acute dacryocystitis, not orbital cellulitis. While dacryocystitis can occasionally seed an orbital infection, tenderness alone over the sac does not distinguish preseptal from orbital cellulitis.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key distinction between preseptal and orbital cellulitis is the orbital septum. Features of post-septal involvement — proptosis, restricted/painful extraocular movements, reduced vision — are the red flags. Normal motility with intact vision and no proptosis points to preseptal disease.
Well done. The triad of proptosis, restricted eye movements, and pain on gaze is the hallmark of orbital (post-septal) cellulitis and mandates urgent CT orbit and IV antibiotics.
